claim: Decisions are influenced by recent experience.
source: Decisions are influenced by recent experience, but the neural basis for this phenomenon is not well understood.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that frames the research question, drawing on established scientific understanding.

claim: The pedunculopontine tegmental nucleus (PPTg) provides input to several nuclei in the action selection network.
source: We focused on activity in the pedunculopontine tegmental nucleus (PPTg), a mesencephalic region that provides input to several nuclei in the action selection network, in well-trained mice selecting actions based on sensory cues and recent trial history.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge about PPTg connectivity.

claim: At the time of action selection, the activity of many PPTg neurons reflected the action on the previous trial and its outcome.
source: We found that, at the time of action selection, the activity of many PPTg neurons reflected the action on the previous trial and its outcome, and the strength of this activity predicted the upcoming choice.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the electrophysiological recordings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The strength of PPTg activity reflecting previous trial information predicted the upcoming choice.
source: We found that, at the time of action selection, the activity of many PPTg neurons reflected the action on the previous trial and its outcome, and the strength of this activity predicted the upcoming choice.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the correlation analysis between neural activity and behavior.

claim: Inactivating the PPTg decreased the influence of recent experience on action selection.
source: Further, inactivating the PPTg predictably decreased the influence of recent experience on action selection.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the pharmacological manipulation experiments.

claim: PPTg input to downstream motor regions provides a mechanism for incorporating recent experience into action selection computations.
source: These findings suggest that PPTg input to downstream motor regions, where it can be integrated with other relevant information, provides a simple mechanism for incorporating recent experience into the computations underlying action selection.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings, involving inference about the mechanism.

claim: Integrating sensory input and internally-generated estimates of action value is well-described by a Bayesian framework.
source: Integrating these sources of information is well-described by a Bayesian framework in which estimates of action value are continually updated by incoming sensory information in order to select the most valuable action (Körding and Wolpert, 2006; Gold and Shadlen, 2007; Kim and Basso, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Updating of action values based on experiencing outcomes is thought to be mediated primarily by striatal circuits.
source: This updating of action values, based on experiencing the outcomes associated with past actions, is thought to be mediated primarily by striatal circuits (Lau and Glimcher, 2007, 2008; Histed et al., 2009; Tai et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Action values can be maintained in striatal activity and used to bias activity in downstream motor centers.
source: These action values can be maintained in striatal activity and ultimately used to bias activity in downstream motor centers such that the most valuable actions are more likely to be selected (Hikosaka et al., 2006, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The superior colliculus (SC) plays a critical role in selecting leftward or rightward orienting movements in the odor-guided spatial choice task.
source: We have previously shown that the superior colliculus (SC) plays a critical role in selecting the action – a leftward or rightward orienting movement – required by this task (Felsen and Mainen, 2008, 2012; Stubblefield et al., 2013), consistent with its role in selecting orienting movements in other species (Glimcher and Sparks, 1992; Horwitz and Newsome, 2001; Bergeron et al., 2003; Krauzlis et al., 2004; Song et al., 2011; Wolf et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to the authors' previous work and work in other species.

claim: The PPTg provides direct input to the SC.
source: In this study, we asked whether the pedunculopontine tegmental nucleus (PPTg), a mesencephalic sensorimotor hub that provides direct input to the SC (Graybiel, 1978; Beninato and Spencer, 1986; Stubblefield et al., 2015), encodes information about recent actions and their outcomes by recording from individual neurons in behaving mice.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: The PPTg is engaged by sensorimotor tasks across species.
source: While numerous regions provide input to the SC (Sparks and Hartwich-Young, 1989), many of which may modulate its processing underlying action selection (Wolf et al., 2015), the PPTg holds particular interest because it is engaged by sensorimotor tasks across species (Matsumura et al., 1997; Dormont et al., 1998; Kobayashi and Isa, 2002; Kobayashi et al., 2002; Okada and Kobayashi, 2009; Norton et al., 2011; Thompson and Felsen, 2013; Lau et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work across multiple species.

claim: Actions in the odor-guided spatial choice task are influenced by actions and outcomes in the recent past.
source: We found that actions in this task are influenced by actions and outcomes in the recent past.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the behavioral analysis.

claim: Most PPTg neurons represented the choice, outcome, or both on the previous trial at the time of action selection and throughout much of the trial.
source: Further, at the time of action selection and even throughout much of the trial, most PPTg neurons represented the choice (left or right movement), outcome (rewarded or non-rewarded), or both, on the previous trial.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The probability of particular upcoming choices was predictably related to the firing rates of neurons selective for choice on the previous trial.
source: Furthermore, we found that these representations influenced action selection: the probability of particular upcoming choices was predictably related to the firing rates of neurons selective for choice on the previous trial, and pharmacological inactivation of the PPTg causally affected behavior, in part by decreasing the influence of recent choices on upcoming choices.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the correlation analysis between neural activity and behavior.

claim: Pharmacological inactivation of the PPTg causally affected behavior by decreasing the influence of recent choices on upcoming choices.
source: Furthermore, we found that these representations influenced action selection: the probability of particular upcoming choices was predictably related to the firing rates of neurons selective for choice on the previous trial, and pharmacological inactivation of the PPTg causally affected behavior, in part by decreasing the influence of recent choices on upcoming choices.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the pharmacological manipulation experiments.

claim: Mice tended to choose the left port more often when they had chosen the left port on the previous trial and had been rewarded.
source: As illustrated in the example data from one mouse in Figure 1B,C, the mouse tended to choose the left port more often when it had chosen the left port on the previous trial and had been rewarded (Figure 1B, compare solid black line to gray line), and tended to choose the right port more often when it had chosen the right port on the previous trial whether or not it had been rewarded (Figure 1C, compare solid and dashed black lines to gray line).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral analysis, illustrated in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Mice tended to choose the right port more often when they had chosen the right port on the previous trial whether or not they had been rewarded.
source: As illustrated in the example data from one mouse in Figure 1B,C, the mouse tended to choose the left port more often when it had chosen the left port on the previous trial and had been rewarded (Figure 1B, compare solid black line to gray line), and tended to choose the right port more often when it had chosen the right port on the previous trial whether or not it had been rewarded (Figure 1C, compare solid and dashed black lines to gray line).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral analysis, illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Mice tended to choose the same side as they had on the previous trial.
source: Consistent with the example data shown in Figure 1B,C, and with some previous work (Lau and Glimcher, 2005), we found that, while there was some variability across mice, they tended to choose the same side as they had on the previous trial (reflected in positive values of  β Choice1) [although in different tasks, a tendency to choose the opposite side has been observed (Lau and Glimcher, 2005; Kim et al., 2007; Sul et al., 2011)], and that this tendency was enhanced when the mouse was rewarded on the previous trial (reflected in positive values of β Outcome: L1 and negative values of β Outcome: R1; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral analysis using logistic regression, illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: The tendency to choose the same side as on the previous trial was enhanced when the mouse was rewarded on the previous trial.
source: Consistent with the example data shown in Figure 1B,C, and with some previous work (Lau and Glimcher, 2005), we found that, while there was some variability across mice, they tended to choose the same side as they had on the previous trial (reflected in positive values of  β Choice1) [although in different tasks, a tendency to choose the opposite side has been observed (Lau and Glimcher, 2005; Kim et al., 2007; Sul et al., 2011)], and that this tendency was enhanced when the mouse was rewarded on the previous trial (reflected in positive values of β Outcome: L1 and negative values of β Outcome: R1; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral analysis using logistic regression, illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: Including the choice and outcome on the previous trial improved the predictive accuracy of the behavioral model for five of seven mice.
source: We found that including the choice and outcome on the previous trial improved the predictive accuracy of the model for five of seven mice (Figure 1E, p<0.0001, one-tailed paired Student's t test separately by mouse).
evidence: This is a finding from the model comparison analysis, illustrated in Figure 1E.

claim: Including the choice and outcome from two trials back did not further improve the predictive accuracy of the model in any mice.
source: However, including the choice and outcome from two trials back did not further improve the predictive accuracy of the model in any mice (Figure 1F, p>0.16, one-tailed paired Student's t test).
evidence: This is a finding from the model comparison analysis, illustrated in Figure 1F.

claim: Movement duration did not depend on the previous choice in most cases.
source: However, we found that this was not the case (durations for rightward movements preceded by right choices and preceded by left choices, analyzed separately for each mouse, did not differ in 7/7 mice; durations for leftward movements preceded by right choices and preceded by left choices did not differ in 6/7 mice; p>0.05, two-tailed unpaired Students t-tests separately by mouse).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of movement duration.

claim: Choices in the task are influenced by what happened on the previous trial, primarily by the choice rather than the outcome.
source: Together, these results indicate that choices in our task are influenced by what happened on the previous trial – primarily by the choice rather than the outcome – and little influenced by the choice or the outcome from two trials in the past.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the behavioral analyses.

claim: Choices in the task are little influenced by the choice or outcome from two trials in the past.
source: Together, these results indicate that choices in our task are influenced by what happened on the previous trial – primarily by the choice rather than the outcome – and little influenced by the choice or the outcome from two trials in the past.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the behavioral analyses.

claim: Few PPTg neurons exhibited a preference for choice on the current trial during the pre-stimulus epoch.
source: We found that few neurons exhibited a preference for choice during this epoch (Figure 2, p<0.05, Monte Carlo permutation test).
evidence: This is a finding from the preference analysis of neural data, illustrated in Figure 2C.

claim: Few PPTg neurons exhibited outcome preference during the pre-stimulus epoch.
source: We found that few neurons exhibited outcome preference (Figure 2, p<0.05).
evidence: This is a finding from the preference analysis of neural data, illustrated in Figure 2D.

claim: A sizeable fraction of PPTg neurons exhibited a preference for the choice on the previous trial during the pre-stimulus epoch.
source: Across the population, a sizeable fraction of neurons exhibited a preference for the choice (Figure 2G; 26% preferred ipsilateral, 49% preferred contralateral, p<0.05; more preferred contralateral than ipsilateral, p=0.001, χ2 test) and outcome (Figure 2H; 46% were selective, p<0.05) on the previous trial.
evidence: This is a finding from the preference analysis of neural data, illustrated in Figure 2G.

claim: A sizeable fraction of PPTg neurons exhibited a preference for the outcome on the previous trial during the pre-stimulus epoch.
source: Across the population, a sizeable fraction of neurons exhibited a preference for the choice (Figure 2G; 26% preferred ipsilateral, 49% preferred contralateral, p<0.05; more preferred contralateral than ipsilateral, p=0.001, χ2 test) and outcome (Figure 2H; 46% were selective, p<0.05) on the previous trial.
evidence: This is a finding from the preference analysis of neural data, illustrated in Figure 2H.

claim: More PPTg neurons preferred contralateral than ipsilateral choices on the previous trial.
source: Across the population, a sizeable fraction of neurons exhibited a preference for the choice (Figure 2G; 26% preferred ipsilateral, 49% preferred contralateral, p<0.05; more preferred contralateral than ipsilateral, p=0.001, χ2 test) and outcome (Figure 2H; 46% were selective, p<0.05) on the previous trial.
evidence: This is a finding from the preference analysis of neural data, illustrated in Figure 2G.

claim: There is a modest correlation between preference for the choice on the previous and current trials.
source: We found a modest correlation between preference for the choice on the previous (Figure 2G) and current (Figure 2C) trials (r = 0.25, p=1.42 × 10−8).
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis of neural preferences.

claim: Two-thirds of PPTg neurons maintained their preference for which reward port was chosen during movement to and from the reward port.
source: We found that, rather than representing movement direction, two-thirds of neurons maintained their preference for which reward port was chosen (p=9.12 × 10−6, χ2 test), suggesting that the preference of PPTg neurons for previous choice (Figure 2G) cannot be accounted for by a dependence on movement direction.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of neural activity during movements in opposite directions.

claim: The preference of PPTg neurons for previous choice cannot be accounted for by a dependence on movement direction.
source: We found that, rather than representing movement direction, two-thirds of neurons maintained their preference for which reward port was chosen (p=9.12 × 10−6, χ2 test), suggesting that the preference of PPTg neurons for previous choice (Figure 2G) cannot be accounted for by a dependence on movement direction.
evidence: This is an inference from the analysis of neural activity during movements in opposite directions.

claim: Few PPTg neurons exhibited a preference for choice or outcome two trials back during the pre-stimulus epoch.
source: We then calculated choice and outcome preference with respect to two trials back (Figure 2I–L) and found that, as was the case for the current trial, few neurons exhibited a preference for choice (Figure 2K) or outcome (Figure 2L), consistent with the relatively little influence on behavior of the choice and outcome from two trials in the past (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a finding from the preference analysis of neural data, illustrated in Figure 2K,L.

claim: A larger proportion of PPTg neurons exhibited a preference for choice or outcome one trial back than on either the current trial or two trials back.
source: Thus, a larger proportion of neurons exhibited a preference for choice or outcome one trial back than on either the current trial or two trials back (choice, p=2.0 × 10–48; outcome, p=3.0 × 10–5, Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA; post-hoc comparisons: choice, one trial back vs. current trial, p=5.6 × 10–30; one trial back vs. two trials back, p=1.6 × 10–30; outcome, one trial back vs. current trial, p=4.0 × 10–4; one trial back vs. two trials back, p=0.002), and there were no differences between the fractions of neurons exhibiting a preference for choice or outcome on the current trial and two trials back (choice, two trials back vs. current trial, p=0.92; outcome, two trials back vs. current trial, p = 0.99).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical comparison of neural preferences across different trial lags.

claim: There were no differences between the fractions of PPTg neurons exhibiting a preference for choice or outcome on the current trial and two trials back.
source: Thus, a larger proportion of neurons exhibited a preference for choice or outcome one trial back than on either the current trial or two trials back (choice, p=2.0 × 10–48; outcome, p=3.0 × 10–5, Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA; post-hoc comparisons: choice, one trial back vs. current trial, p=5.6 × 10–30; one trial back vs. two trials back, p=1.6 × 10–30; outcome, one trial back vs. current trial, p=4.0 × 10–4; one trial back vs. two trials back, p=0.002), and there were no differences between the fractions of neurons exhibiting a preference for choice or outcome on the current trial and two trials back (choice, two trials back vs. current trial, p=0.92; outcome, two trials back vs. current trial, p = 0.99).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical comparison of neural preferences across different trial lags.

claim: PPTg activity during the pre-stimulus epoch is primarily modulated by the choice and outcome on the previous trial.
source: These results suggest that PPTg activity during the pre-stimulus epoch is primarily modulated by the choice and outcome on the previous trial (although our analyses again cannot entirely rule out the possibility that body position also modulates neural activity).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the preference analyses, with a caveat about body position.

claim: PPTg activity in epochs other than the pre-stimulus epoch reflects the choice and outcome on the current trial.
source: Previous work using the same task has shown that PPTg activity in other epochs reflects the choice and outcome on the current trial (Thompson and Felsen, 2013), consistent with other studies of PPTg function (Matsumura et al., 1997; Dormont et al., 1998; Kobayashi et al., 2002; Norton et al., 2011; Maclaren et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The influence of the previous trial on PPTg activity declines by the time the mouse exits the odor port.
source: The influence of the previous trial declines by the time the mouse exits the odor port (Figure 3A, middle), and the influence of the current choice increases upon reward port entry (Figure 3A, right), consistent with the fact that many neurons exhibit preference for the current choice during and following entrance to the reward port (Thompson and Felsen, 2013).
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis of neural data over time, illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: The influence of the current choice on PPTg activity increases upon reward port entry.
source: The influence of the previous trial declines by the time the mouse exits the odor port (Figure 3A, middle), and the influence of the current choice increases upon reward port entry (Figure 3A, right), consistent with the fact that many neurons exhibit preference for the current choice during and following entrance to the reward port (Thompson and Felsen, 2013).
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis of neural data over time, illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: Initially, even preceding odor delivery, the activity of many PPTg neurons reflects the choice on the previous trial, while the activity of virtually no neurons reflects the choice on the current trial.
source: Initially – even preceding odor delivery – the activity of many neurons reflects the choice on the previous trial, while the activity of virtually no neurons reflects the choice on the current trial (Figure 3C, left).
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis of neural data over time, illustrated in Figure 3C.

claim: During stimulus presentation many PPTg neurons begin to reflect the choice on the current trial.
source: During stimulus presentation many neurons begin to reflect the choice on the current trial, and by the time the movement is initiated more neurons reflect the choice on the current than the previous trial (Figure 3C, middle).
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis of neural data over time, illustrated in Figure 3C.

claim: By the time the movement is initiated more PPTg neurons reflect the choice on the current than the previous trial.
source: During stimulus presentation many neurons begin to reflect the choice on the current trial, and by the time the movement is initiated more neurons reflect the choice on the current than the previous trial (Figure 3C, middle).
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis of neural data over time, illustrated in Figure 3C.

claim: The choice on the current trial retains its influence on PPTg activity for the remainder of the trial while the influence of the choice on the previous trial declines.
source: The choice on the current trial retains its influence for the remainder of the trial while the influence of the choice on the previous trial declines (Figure 3C, right), although, interestingly, a sizeable fraction of neurons continues to reflect the choice on the previous trial until well-after the mouse has made its choice on the current trial.
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis of neural data over time, illustrated in Figure 3C.

claim: A sizeable fraction of PPTg neurons continues to reflect the choice on the previous trial until well-after the mouse has made its choice on the current trial.
source: The choice on the current trial retains its influence for the remainder of the trial while the influence of the choice on the previous trial declines (Figure 3C, right), although, interestingly, a sizeable fraction of neurons continues to reflect the choice on the previous trial until well-after the mouse has made its choice on the current trial.
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis of neural data over time, illustrated in Figure 3C.

claim: The activity of more PPTg neurons is more strongly influenced by previous trial outcome early in the trial, and by current trial outcome later in the trial.
source: Similar to the evolving representation of choice, the activity of more neurons is more strongly influenced by previous trial outcome early in the trial (Figure 3D,E, left), and by current trial outcome later in the trial (Figure 3D,E, right).
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis of neural data over time, illustrated in Figure 3D,E.

claim: Virtually no PPTg neurons represent previous outcome by the time the mouse initiates its movement to the reward port.
source: In contrast to the long-lasting representation of previous choice (Figure 3B,C), virtually none of these neurons represent previous outcome by the time the mouse initiates its movement to the reward port (Figure 3D,E, middle; however, note that the population of neurons analyzed was selected based on preference for previous choice, and not previous outcome, during the pre-stimulus epoch).
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis of neural data over time, illustrated in Figure 3D,E.

claim: PPTg activity evolves from representing information about the previous trial to representing information about the current trial.
source: These analyses show how PPTg activity evolves from representing information about the previous trial to representing information about the current trial, which may reflect the transfer of previous-trial information from the PPTg to a downstream region where it can be integrated with sensory evidence in order to form a motor plan.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the regression analyses, with an inference about the functional significance.

claim: The evolution of PPTg activity may reflect the transfer of previous-trial information from the PPTg to a downstream region where it can be integrated with sensory evidence to form a motor plan.
source: These analyses show how PPTg activity evolves from representing information about the previous trial to representing information about the current trial, which may reflect the transfer of previous-trial information from the PPTg to a downstream region where it can be integrated with sensory evidence in order to form a motor plan.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the temporal dynamics of neural activity.

claim: Many more PPTg neurons exhibited a significantly positive slope than negative slope in the relationship between firing rate and current choice on ambiguous trials.
source: Across this population of neurons, many more exhibited a significantly positive slope than negative slope (p<0.05, Monte Carlo permutation test; positive slopes: 136/378; negative slopes: 30/378; positive > negative, p=0.001, χ2 test; Figure 4B), indicating a similar relationship between firing rate and current choice as shown in Figure 4A.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of the relationship between neural activity and choice, illustrated in Figure 4B.

claim: Each mouse exhibited more PPTg neurons with positive than negative slopes in the relationship between firing rate and current choice.
source: To determine whether this was the case, we examined the distribution of slopes separately for each mouse and found that each exhibited more neurons with positive than negative slopes (Figure 4C), even though the behavior of some mice did not depend on previous choice (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of the relationship between neural activity and choice, illustrated in Figure 4C.

claim: The representation of the choice on the previous trial can directly influence the choice made by the mouse on the current trial.
source: These results suggest that the representation of the choice on the previous trial (Figure 2) can directly influence the choice made by the mouse on the current trial.
evidence: This is an inference from the analysis showing that neural activity predicts choice even in mice whose behavior does not depend on previous choice.

claim: Unilateral PPTg inactivation resulted in choices biased ipsilateral to the inactivated PPTg.
source: We found that choices were biased ipsilateral to the inactivated PPTg, as compared to the preceding and following control sessions in which saline was infused to the same PPTg (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from the pharmacological inactivation experiments, illustrated in Figure 5A.

claim: Unilaterally inactivating the PPTg resulted in a modest ipsilateral influence on choices.
source: We found that unilaterally inactivating the PPTg resulted in a modest ipsilateral influence on choices (Figure 5B; p<0.05, two-tailed unpaired Student's t test, pooled across 3 animals and 30 sets of sessions (424 ± 105 trials; mean ± STD); βMuscimol > 0 in 14/30 individual sets of sessions, βMuscimol < 0 in 6/30 individual sets of sessions, p<0.05, two-tailed one-sample Student's t test; black bars), indicating a causal relationship between PPTg activity and contralateral movements in this task.
evidence: This is a finding from the pharmacological inactivation experiments, illustrated in Figure 5B.

claim: There is a causal relationship between PPTg activity and contralateral movements in the odor-guided spatial choice task.
source: We found that unilaterally inactivating the PPTg resulted in a modest ipsilateral influence on choices (Figure 5B; p<0.05, two-tailed unpaired Student's t test, pooled across 3 animals and 30 sets of sessions (424 ± 105 trials; mean ± STD); βMuscimol > 0 in 14/30 individual sets of sessions, βMuscimol < 0 in 6/30 individual sets of sessions, p<0.05, two-tailed one-sample Student's t test; black bars), indicating a causal relationship between PPTg activity and contralateral movements in this task.
evidence: This is an inference from the pharmacological inactivation experiments.

claim: Movement latency and duration were longer in muscimol than in saline sessions.
source: Consistent with the modest but significant effect of unilateral inactivation on choice bias, we found that movement latency and duration – both to and from the reward port – were longer in muscimol than in saline sessions, even when contralateral and ipsilateral choices were pooled (Materials and methods; p=4.55 × 10−20, 5.24 × 10−32, and 0.0026, respectively, two-tailed unpaired Student's t tests).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of movement timing in the pharmacological inactivation experiments.

claim: PPTg activity representing previous experience influences action selection.
source: These results support our hypothesis that the PPTg activity representing previous experience (Figure 2) influences action selection.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the pharmacological inactivation experiments.

claim: Behavior in the stimulus-cued spatial-choice task can be accounted for by a Bayesian framework in which choices are influenced by both recent trial history and the sensory stimulus.
source: We first found that behavior in a stimulus-cued spatial-choice task can be accounted for by a Bayesian framework (among others) in which choices are influenced by both recent trial history and the sensory stimulus (Figure 1), consistent with previous studies (Gold et al., 2008; Busse et al., 2011; Akaishi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the behavioral analyses, supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Activity of a subpopulation of PPTg neurons reflects choices and outcomes in the recent past and correlated with upcoming choice.
source: We then found that activity of a subpopulation of PPTg neurons reflects choices and outcomes in the recent past (Figures 2 and 3) and correlated with upcoming choice (Figure 4), suggesting a role in mediating the influence of recent experience on behavior.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the electrophysiological analyses.

claim: The PPTg encodes representations of recent experience that can contribute to action selection.
source: Together, our results demonstrate that the PPTg encodes representations of recent experience that can contribute to action selection.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from all the experimental findings.

claim: The motor-related role of the PPTg has traditionally been considered in the context of central pattern generation.
source: The motor-related role of the PPTg has traditionally been considered in the context of central pattern generation (Garcia-Rill, 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: PPTg activity encodes specific actions and reflects their outcomes.
source: More recent studies in behaving animals have found that PPTg activity encodes specific actions and reflects their outcomes (Matsumura et al., 1997; Dormont et al., 1998; Okada and Kobayashi, 2009; Norton et al., 2011; Maclaren et al., 2013; Thompson and Felsen, 2013) and have suggested that the PPTg may be involved in attention and other cognitive processes (Steckler et al., 1994; Winn, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The PPTg may be involved in attention and other cognitive processes.
source: More recent studies in behaving animals have found that PPTg activity encodes specific actions and reflects their outcomes (Matsumura et al., 1997; Dormont et al., 1998; Okada and Kobayashi, 2009; Norton et al., 2011; Maclaren et al., 2013; Thompson and Felsen, 2013) and have suggested that the PPTg may be involved in attention and other cognitive processes (Steckler et al., 1994; Winn, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: PPTg output may play a role in providing information about recent actions and their outcomes that can be used to guide the selection of actions mediated by downstream motor circuits.
source: The results described here are consistent with these findings and suggest that PPTg output may play a role in providing information about recent actions and their outcomes that can be used to guide the selection of actions mediated by downstream motor circuits.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings, involving speculation about the functional role of PPTg.

claim: Downstream circuits do not necessarily utilize PPTg information about recent experience, given that it is represented in PPTg activity even in mice that do not exhibit a behavioral dependence on previous choice.
source: However, downstream circuits do not necessarily utilize this information, given that it is represented in PPTg activity even in mice that do not exhibit a behavioral dependence on previous choice (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that neural representations exist even when behavior does not depend on previous choice.

claim: The PPTg projects to several motor-related regions including other brainstem nuclei and the striatum.
source: While the PPTg projects to several motor-related regions including other brainstem nuclei and the striatum (Beninato and Spencer, 1987; Inglis and Winn, 1995), and the current study cannot rule out the involvement of these regions, an attractive candidate is the SC.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: The SC is an attractive candidate for where PPTg representations of recent experience might be conveyed to modulate action selection.
source: While the PPTg projects to several motor-related regions including other brainstem nuclei and the striatum (Beninato and Spencer, 1987; Inglis and Winn, 1995), and the current study cannot rule out the involvement of these regions, an attractive candidate is the SC.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the downstream target of PPTg projections.

claim: Cholinergic PPTg neurons project to and excite neurons in the SC responsible for motor output.
source: Cholinergic PPTg neurons project to and excite neurons in the SC responsible for motor output (Beninato and Spencer, 1986; Sooksawate et al., 2008; Stubblefield et al., 2015), and nicotinic signaling in the SC has been shown to modulate orienting behavior (Weldon et al., 1983; Aizawa et al., 1999; Watanabe et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous anatomical and physiological studies.

claim: Nicotinic signaling in the SC has been shown to modulate orienting behavior.
source: Cholinergic PPTg neurons project to and excite neurons in the SC responsible for motor output (Beninato and Spencer, 1986; Sooksawate et al., 2008; Stubblefield et al., 2015), and nicotinic signaling in the SC has been shown to modulate orienting behavior (Weldon et al., 1983; Aizawa et al., 1999; Watanabe et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The SC is thought to integrate a wide range of inputs in order to select orienting actions.
source: The SC is thought to integrate a wide range of inputs in order to select orienting actions (Kobayashi and Isa, 2002; Krauzlis et al., 2004; Grossberg et al., 2015; Wolf et al., 2015) and is thus well-positioned to combine – possibly additively – incoming sensory information with prior representations of action value (provided before, during, or even after the onset of sensory input; Figure 3B,C) in order to select the most valuable action (Trappenberg et al., 2001; Dorris et al., 2007; Kim and Basso, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The source of prior representations of action value in the SC may be the PPTg.
source: Our results suggest that the source of these prior representations may be the PPTg, which could complement other SC inputs – such as inhibition from the basal ganglia (Hikosaka and Wurtz, 1983; Chevalier et al., 1985) – in biasing action selection by modulating SC processing according to recently-experienced action-value associations (Kobayashi and Isa, 2002; Hikosaka et al., 2006; Wolf et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings about the functional role of PPTg input to SC.

claim: Representations of trial history similar to that in PPTg have been observed in the striatum, prefrontal cortex, and premotor cortex.
source: Given the importance of trial history for action selection, it is not surprising that representations of trial history similar to that shown here have been observed in several brain areas, including the striatum (Lau and Glimcher, 2007, 2008; Histed et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2013), prefrontal cortex (Histed et al., 2009) and premotor cortex (Marcos et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Activity in the striatum, prefrontal cortex, and premotor cortex typically reflects information from several previous trials.
source: Activity in these regions typically reflects information from several previous trials, while PPTg activity was primarily associated with the immediately preceding trial (Figure 2).
evidence: This statement contrasts the findings in PPTg with previous work in other brain regions, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: PPTg activity was primarily associated with the immediately preceding trial.
source: Activity in these regions typically reflects information from several previous trials, while PPTg activity was primarily associated with the immediately preceding trial (Figure 2).

claim: The representations in the PPTg suggest a complementary mechanism to the more computationally expensive processing in other regions for integrating internal representations of experience with sensory evidence.
source: While this difference may be due to different task demands (recall that tracking past trials conferred no behavioral benefit in our task), the representations in the PPTg that we observed suggest a complementary mechanism to the more computationally expensive processing in these other regions for integrating internal representations of experience with sensory evidence: Specifically, that PPTg directly influences the circuits underlying action selection based on recent experience, which may be well-suited to the relevant dynamics of some real-world situations.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the findings.

claim: Behavior in similar tasks is often influenced by previous trials in mice, primates and humans.
source: Although optimal performance on this task requires that choices be based only on the current stimulus, previous studies – in mice, primates and humans – have shown that behavior in such tasks is, nevertheless, often influenced by previous trials (Lau and Glimcher, 2005; Gold et al., 2008; Busse et al., 2011; Akaishi et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: 506 PPTg neurons were recorded across the seven mice.
source: To quantify dependence on choice across the population of 506 PPTg neurons recorded, we used an ROC-based preference analysis that uses the firing rates in a particular epoch to assign values ranging from −1 (ipsilateral preference) to 1 (contralateral preference), where the magnitude reflects preference strength (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the sample size for the electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The pre-stimulus epoch is from odor port entry to 100 ms after odor valve open.
source: We were initially interested in preference during the pre-stimulus epoch – from odor port entry to 100 ms after odor valve open (Figure 1A, gray shading; Figure 2A, gray bar) – when the mouse is presumably preparing to update its estimates of the value of each option (i.e., to move left or right) with the information provided by the stimulus.
evidence: This is a description of the temporal epoch used for analysis, illustrated in Figure 1A and Figure 2A.
